item.title: Search Feature For Static Websites
item.description: I've just added a search feature to this website. The website is static, but it is built programmatically. After switching my build process over to a PHP one, the process of adding a search feature was actually pretty simple. It doesn't require PHP, you just need a way to set up a JSON object with the content you want to make searchable. I'll go over how I did it in this post.
item.content:encoded:
I've just added a search feature to this website. The website is static, but it is built programmatically. After switching my build process over to a PHP one, the process of adding a search feature was actually pretty simple. It doesn't require PHP, you just need a way to set up a JSON object with the content you want to make searchable. I'll go over how I did it in this post.

There are a few ways to achieve this. Google offer a programmable search engine if you have a static site that you want to make searchable but aren't very technically adept, or just want it done quickly. I don't want large scripts or services I don't control in my website so that's a no for me. Apache offer Solr if you want to host your own search index. I might return to look at this once I have a bit more experience setting up Docker images on my Coolify instance, and if the data collection on my website becomes so large that static searching becomes impractical. And then there's static searching; indexing the data within the client itself, and offloading the work to the users browser.

I want my site to work well and do it fast. So that had some influence on how I executed the process, and on which search tool I chose. Two standouts were FlexSearch and MiniSearch. But I went with Lunr, which was just easier to get going with a static file that I can keep on my own site. There are comments floating around StackOverflow pointing out that the project hasn't had an update since 2020, but since I'm not using NodeJS here, and the script itself appears safe, it shouldn't cause any issues.

Getting Started

First and foremost, we need the data we want to search. I used PHP for this and simply write the return value into a JSON file in my build script. I will also want to manipulate DOM to show results, so I will include a few extra bits to help with that.

<?php

$configs = include CONFIG_PATH . 'config.php';
require APP_PATH . 'helpers.php';
$posts = [];
$jsonResponse = array();

foreach ($configs['blogs'] as $blog => $blogDesc) {
    $posts += [...getBlogPosts($blog)];
}

foreach ($posts as $path => $post) {
  $content = getPostText($post['dom']);
  $postInfo = getPostInfo($post['dom']);
  [
    'title' => $title,
    'description' => $description,
    'date' => $date
  ] = $postInfo;


  $jsonResponse[$path] = [
    'url' => $path,
    'blog' => ucfirst($post['blog']),
    'textContent' => trim($content),
    'title' => $title,
    'description' => $description,
    'date' => $date,
    'dateString' => formatDate($date)
  ];
}
     
header('Content-Type: application/json;');
echo json_encode($jsonResponse);

This is the controller for my search/feed route in my static site generator. There's a few helper functions here doing most of the work with regard to organising the data, but essentially I'm just collecting the posts from all my blogs, getting a stripped down version of the text (I'm only including text within p elements and ignoring all else), getting a few helpful DOM extractions, and then sending that data in a JSON response, in the form of an array of objects. Writing that to a file is one line in the terminal, or a line in my BASH build script.

php index.php "search/feed" > dist/search/feed.json

Setting Up Search

How you execute the process is entirely up to you. I opted to keep it simple, and delegate as little work to the client as I could get away with while still having a functional search feature. I also plan for JavaScript to be disabled by the user or not to load. Here is a mildly entertaining post listing reasons why that might happen; the train tunnel phenomenon is something I occasionally experience as my commute to work goes underground a few times en route. So I went with a search form on the home page, which is hidden until the clients browser detects JavaScript, that directs a query to a search page where the search is actually executed.

<search id="search" class="noscript">
  <form action="/search">
    <input type="text" name="query" required placeholder="Search posts...">
    <button type="submit">Search</button>
  </form>
</search>

That snippet is actually a PHP partial that I can require in my home page and my search page. So later I can make changes to one block of code and have it persist wherever it is used.

Next we need the actual lunr file itself. The full static file can be found in the projects GitHub, and the guide offers an unpkg CDN file, but it's the full file, which is quite large. It's very well documented using JSDoc comments. I haven't seen it mentioned in the guide, but there is a minified version available from the unpkg CDN too. So I downloaded that straight into my project's files.

curl -o assets/scripts/lunr.js https://unpkg.com/lunr@2.3.9/lunr.min.js

Next, after including the script in the search page, we just need to fetch our JSON feed and build an index. There are extras available such as match indices and fuzzy search, but I explained in my blog why I opted to just use the defaults. So with the following in our own search.js we are ready to get started with setting up the rest of the page's functionality.

async function getFeed(url) {
  try {
    const response = await fetch(url);
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Response status: ${response.status}`);
    }

    const result = await response.json();

    return result;
  } catch (error) {
    console.log(error.message);
    return null;
  }
}
  
function getIdx(feed) {
  const idx = lunr(function () {
    this.ref('url');
    this.field('title');
    this.field('textContent');
    
    for (const item in feed) {
      this.add(feed[item]);
    }
  })

  return idx;
}
  
// perform a search
const feed = await getFeed('/search/feed.json');
const idx = getIdx(feed);
const results = idx.search(query);

Setting Up The Page Functionality

I've gotten into the habit of using classes when a bunch of code works together to achieve a single concept. Such as searching content. So I will be using a JavaScript class, while not telling you that OOP will change your life. If you prefer to work functionally, you will likely be passing a lot more parameters into functions if you aren't scoping globally (oops! Sorry, I literally just said I wouldn't do that).

Before we write any more script let's arrange our HTML first. We need the search form, and somewhere to put the results. I've chosen not to list results in an unordered list, but to present them as articles with links as I would in a blog page, so I'm breaking one of my own rules in this case and actually using a div element.

<search id="search" class="noscript">
  <form action="/search">
    <input type="text" name="query" required placeholder="Search posts...">
    <button type="submit">Search</button>
  </form>
</search>    

<div id="results" class="noscript">
  <h2></h2>
  
  <template id="result">
    <article>
      <header>
        <h3><a href=""></a></h3>
        <time></time>
      </header>
      <p class="description"></p>
      <a href="">Read More</a>
    </article>
  </template>
</div>

I've recently read a pretty good article about memory efficient DOM manipulation, so I'm going to be using a template element for my individual search results. Now that we have a DOM, it's time to write some JavaScript. It's also worth noting the noscript class attached to both elements here. They will be set to display: none in CSS until JavaScript is detected.

class Search {
  constructor(feed, idx) {
    this.feed = feed;
    this.idx = idx;
    
    this.resultsElem = document.querySelector('#results');
    this.form = this.document.querySelector('search#search form');
    this.template = results.querySelector('template#result');

    this.domMap = new WeakMap();
  }
}

Starting with just the constructor function for a class of Search, we can pass in the feed and index that we have already defined. In terms of DOM, we will want access to the results div, the search form, and the predefined template. I've also put a WeakMap instance in there, as the DOM will be being created and destroyed on consecutive searches, and a weak map ensures that removed elements are cleared by the garbage collector and don't stick around in memory. The form will need an event listener with preventDefault to prevent page loads when new searches are performed. I like to take care of this in an init method once I know everything is properly set up.

class Search {
  ...  

  init() {
    this.form.addEventListener('submit', evt => {
      evt.preventDefault();
      
      if (this.form.query.value.length > 0) {
        const query = this.form.query.value;
        const url = new URL(window.location);
        
        url.searchParams.set('query', query);
        history.pushState(null, '', url);
        
        this.form.query.value = '';
        document.activeElement.blur();
        
        this.results = this.handleSearch(query);
      }
    });
  } 
}

We prevent the default form action, and an arrow function preserves the this of the class, instead of referring to the event target as it would with a normal function callback. The DOM form object saves us a little work here, and we can ignore the form submission if the forms query value is empty. I set the search params on the url and push them to the history object, this allows the page to operate normally, and the user can cycle back through their previous searches, even though we are preventing page loads on form submission. Next the input value is set back to blank and the elements focus removed, before passing the query into a handleSearch method. Let's write that method now.

class Search {
  ...

  handleSearch(query) {
    this.removeResults();
    
    const results = this.idx.search(query);
    this.populate = this.populateResults(results);
    
    const msg = `Showing ${results.length} results for "${query}"`;
    this.resultsElem.querySelector('h2').textContent = msg;
  }  
}

The handleSearch method calls a removeResults method to remove any search results currently being displayed in the DOM, then performs a search with the provided query. The results are passed into a populateResults method to add them to the DOM. Finally a message is passed into the h2 element of the results div to explain to the user just what they are looking at exactly.

class Search {
  ...

  removeResults() {
    const results = this.resultsElem.querySelectorAll('article');
    results.forEach(i => i.remove());
  }
 
}

The removeResults method is quite simple, yet also quite powerful when combined with the weak map instance we defined in the constructor. It requires that elements are set in to the weak map first, as we will do in the populateResults method. But essentially it will strip all removed elements from memory via the garbage collector.

class Search {
  ...
  
  populateResults(results) {
    for (const result of results) {
      const post = this.feed[result['ref']];
      const url = post['url'] + '/';
     
      const clone = document.importNode(this.template.content, true);
      this.domMap.set(clone);
      
      const h3 = clone.querySelector('h3 > a');
      h3.textContent = `${post['title']} [${post['blog']}]`;
      h3.href = url;
      const timeEl = clone.querySelector('time');
      timeEl.textContent = post['dateString'];
      timeEl.dateTime = post['date'];
      clone.querySelector('p.description').textContent = post['description'];
      clone.querySelector('article > a').href = url;

      this.resultsElem.appendChild(clone);
    }
  } 
}

The populateResults method iterates through the results, while matching the referenced text to the post it was extracted from. It clones the template we defined in the HTML, and adds it to the weak map instance. Then it simply completes the required DOM and appends the newly created article element to the results div.

Since the getIdx and getFeed functions are purely concerned with the search feature, I will move them into the class as well, as static methods, so that they can be executed before an instance is created - since we can't create an instance until we have the data that they both return.

class Search{
...
  static async getFeed(url) {
    try {
      const response = await fetch(url);
      if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(`Response status: ${response.status}`);
      }

      const result = await response.json();

      return result;
    } catch (error) {
      console.log(error.message);
      return null;
    }
  }


  static getIdx(feed) {
    const idx = lunr(function () {
      this.ref('url');
      this.field('title');
      this.field('textContent');
      
      for (const item in feed) {
        this.add(feed[item]);
      }
    })

    return idx;
  }
}

Now everything is set up, we can set up the page controls. Since we are working with DOM, I like to use the DOMContentLoaded event to ensure the script has access to everything it needs upon execution.

document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', async function() {
  const feedUrl = '/search/feed.json';
  const feed = await Search.getFeed(feedUrl);

  if (feed !== null) {
    const idx = Search.getIdx(feed);
    const search = new Search(feed, idx);
    search.init();

  } else {
    const msg = 'Something went wrong, try reloading...';
    document.querySelector('#results h2').textContent = msg;
  }

  document.querySelectorAll('.noscript').forEach(i => {
    i.classList.remove('noscript');
  });
});

Once DOM content has loaded, the feed is fetched. If a feed is returned, instead of the null value that is triggered in the catch statement, then an index is created, and both values get passed into a new instance of Search which is then initialised to apply the search forms event listener. The noscript classes aren't removed until everything else has executed, so if something hangs and blocks the script, the page remains blank. Otherwise, if there's an error, a message will be displayed to the user that something has gone wrong.

URL Based Search Queries

We have a working search page, but we aren't quite finished. We haven't yet accounted for searches performed on the home page that are then routed to the search page via the form's action. Luckily, with the search instance, we have everything we need to achieve this in just a few lines of code.

if (feed !== null) {
  const idx = Search.getIdx(feed);
  const search = new Search(feed, idx);
  search.init();

  const searchParams = new URLSearchParams(window.location.search);
  
  if (searchParams.size > 0) {
    const query = searchParams.get('query');
    search.handleSearch(query);
  }
}

Using the URLSearchParams object, it is simple to pass in the window objects location information, and use that to extract the query and perform a search with the handleSearch method we defined earlier. The method will take care of everything for us including the DOM manipulation.

item.title: My Site Has a Search Feature
item.description: Now my website is running it's development environment and building it's static files using PHP, the process of making modifications has become much easier and more fluid. Because of this, I decided to I would explore the idea of implementing a search feature for my static site. And after about a days work, I now have a search feature!
item.content:encoded:
Now my website is running it's development environment and building it's static files using PHP, the process of making modifications has become much easier and more fluid. Because of this, I decided to I would explore the idea of implementing a search feature for my static site. And after about a days work, I now have a search feature!

When I started researching the idea, I didn't expect it to be quite so .. easy. A quick web search landed me on a recommendation for lunr.js, followed immediately by a warning saying it hasn't been updated since around 2020. I looked around elsewhere, but I came back to take a second look at lunr. It had a frontend JavaScript file I could just download and use, everything else seemed to require Node JS or a CDN script. I'm doing my best to try and keep this project out of the Node JS ecosystem, and external CDN's are a no for me as I want everything in the same place - if the script isn't loading then it's likely that the website won't either, removing the risk of broken dependencies. I suppose I could curl the CDN script into a file, but most other solutions I looked at provide minified versions which are difficult to audit.

So I came back to lunr. I perused the source file just to make sure it wasn't connecting to any external services on the sly (it doesn't), and that was good enough for me. The scariest thing about it is that it uses the old pseudoclass functions - so archaic! The website doesn't make it clear, but there is minified version of the cdn script that can lighten the load since the main script is very well documented - I could learn a thing or two there I guess. So after a curl -o lunr.js https://unpkg.com/lunr@2.3.9/lunr.min.js I was ready to go.

I'm pretty happy with the result. I enjoyed working on it so much that I may do a guide in the near future. I've deployed the changes and eveything seems to be working fine so far. For it to work I had to generate a JSON feed with the text from all the posts across my site, and some additional data to build the DOM. The file is a little heavy at 168.9kB - more than any other file on my website but I'd argue that it's still perfectly acceptable. The JetBrains woff file isn't too far behind at 113.7kB - maybe I should look at a few other ligature monospace fonts? The JSON feed was easy enough to generate with PHP, and of course it's deployed from a static file so it's only ever my machine doing the work prior deployment with regard to the PHP code.

There were some upgrade options, such as fuzzy search and returning indices of the matches. But after experimenting, I decided fuzzy search returns far too many matches for "raspberry pi" - by default it tokenises the query, and pi with a fuzz setting of just 1 becomes far too lenient. The indices might have been helpful if the text samples were smaller. I don't imagine it being too difficult to iterate backwards through the string indices and plug in some mark tags to highlight the matches, but my text samples are just too large so it's not worth it. So I just stuck with the defaults, and I'm just presenting my results as I would a list of posts in any of the blog feeds, albeit without the option to filter topics.

item.title: My Path From Here
item.description: I've been finding time to spend coding recently. I've learned a little PHP and applied it. My energy is high, but my focus and direction are low.
item.content:encoded:
I've been finding time to spend coding recently. I've learned a little PHP and applied it. My energy is high, but my focus and direction are low.

I suppose that this is a post just to keep me mentally on track. I've found time, against the odds, to learn a little PHP and apply it. That's got me excited to be at my computer again. I also migrated my site over to my Coolify server. Migrating and changing my build tools also meant I had to fix a few bugs that slipped through in all the excitement. I also made some quality of life changes to my website, and dusted off an old checklist of a few things I wanted to implement but never got round to, and ticked those all off too.

So I'm here because I started learning PHP. And now my enthusiasm is high but not pointed anywhere in particular, so I'm doing that thing where I get pulled toward anything I find remotely interesting. Distractions. Carry on with PHP - if just the syntax got me this excited then I ought to force myself back on track and keep going.

item.title: Unicorns
item.description: I got unicorns. I've seen a few people raging at GitHub lately, I don't like joining in on politics. But my personal website has been affected now and I've taken action.
item.content:encoded:
I got unicorns. I've seen a few people raging at GitHub lately, I don't like joining in on politics. But my personal website has been affected now and I've taken action.

I'm not leaving GitHub. Not yet anyway. If I did I would most likely move everything over to my GitLab account - I haven't even logged into it for years, but it exists. I've heard a lot of opinions that GitLab is just as bad (as GitHub), but I don't see self-hosting repositories as a solution for me. I already host my own NextCloud and Coolify instances, I can't imagine looking after a versioning hosting server - I am managing my cloud and web server, but I often feel a little out of my depth in doing so. Also, code repositories are something I would prefer not lose - and I'd like the liberty of being able to blame someone else if something were to happen to them.

So, for now, I am still hosting the repository for this website on GitHub, but it's now deployed through my Coolify instance. I had considered moving it to my Netlify account, but Netlify has lambdas, so I would prefer to keep that for projects that require a little more functionality than a standard static website, but don't necessarily require a proper server. There are, of course, other services, but I already have so many accounts for so many things, so I'm making use of what I already have set up for now.

The unicorns. I had heard about them, but not seen them myself. Until a few months ago. If the GitHub servers go down proper, you see the unicorn. It's something to do with their server using software called Unicorn. But I've now adopted the phrase for whenever GitHub doesn't work. The first unicorn was when I tried to make a commit a little while ago, and it wasn't working. So I did a DuckDuckGo search for how to test my GitHub SSH connection to make sure that it was working correctly. The GitHub page with the instructions failed, as did the rest of the website, and there was the majestic creature right on my screen. Yesterday, I commited a new post to my blog, and the GitHub Pages action kept timing out after a few seconds. I couldn't figure out what was wrong. I have a strong suspicion that I'm nowhere near any of the size limits imposed on the free GitHub Pages websites. Furthermore, it was a brand new repository with hardly any history as I had just changed my website management tool to a new one that I had written in PHP to replace my old Python one. There's been speculation that A.I. agents have been reeking havoc on GitHubs servers. Whatever the reason, it might have been fine if I had just waited a few hours, but I do a lot of work on that particular repository and I don't want to have to wait a day to push an update.

Moving the project over to Coolify wasn't too difficult. The NixPacks set up is pretty simple. I can serve from the dist folder now too, which is nice. There were ways to do that with GitHub Pages, but it was just easier to go with the default docs directory and not have to use custom actions. For the site to redeploy on pushes I had to set up a webhook in GitHub, hopefully that is less taxing on their servers than the Github Pages action, and therefore less likely to cause issues later on. Getting the DNS moved over wasn't too tricky either, although I had forgotten what I was doing with the CloudFlare tunnel as it doesn't come up as an option on the DNS configuration page (Coolify is running on a Raspberry Pi on my desk so the usual point at IP and go won't suffice here). I did eventually find it again in the zero trust section, and after copying the values I had set for *.aaronwattts.dev over to aaronwatts.dev, it was just a case of waiting for the new settings to propogate.

So now my website is self-hosted - which is cool, I guess. I've changed the powered by in the footer from GtitHub Pages to Raspberry Pi. They are quite concise about the use of their logo so that's one less SVG for me to worry about. The terms of use apparently apply to the words "Raspberry Pi" too, but I'll risk it, I'm an avid fan of their work and you'll be pressed to find a bad word about them on this website.

item.title: PHP Template Partials
item.description: This won't be long enough to make it into the guides section of my site. But from enquiring with search engines, I couldn't find an answer that gave an answer that was quite complex compared to how a partial normally works, or showed how to do PHP partials with X framework. So I'm including in my blog as a note.
item.content:encoded:
This won't be long enough to make it into the guides section of my site. But from enquiring with search engines, I couldn't find an answer that gave an answer that was quite complex compared to how a partial normally works, or showed how to do PHP partials with X framework. So I'm including in my blog as a note.

I was having trouble working out how to include partials in my PHP templates. But this morning I had that well, duh! moment and rigged some up for my website. The same way I require a template, I just needed to require the partial within the template itself. So now I can make adjustments to things like my footer once, and not have to worry about consistency across pages.

<!-- header.php -->
<header>
  <h1>Welcome to my website!</h1>
</header>

<!-- index.php -->
<html>
  <body>
    <?php require PARTIALS_PATH . 'header.php' ?>
  </body>
</html>

item.title: Hello, World!
item.description: My blog has been abandoned. Welcome to my blog. I have just rebuilt this website's site management tools using PHP. I had intended to import my blog reel from a Publii site that I was using for blogging, with this site featuring more topical posts. But I have decided I will start anew here. Blog reels can fill up fast, after all.
item.content:encoded:
My blog has been abandoned. Welcome to my blog. I have just rebuilt this website's site management tools using PHP. I had intended to import my blog reel from a Publii site that I was using for blogging, with this site featuring more topical posts. But I have decided I will start anew here. Blog reels can fill up fast, after all.

I've stopped using Publii, for now the site still still exists, although I may delete the repository at some point and just let my Cloudflare DNS redirect here. I looked to see if there was an easy way to export from Publii, and came across another recent-ish post by Greg Walsh, about him making a similar decision. I'm pleased he's kept a Simple-ish design similar to the default Publii one. I really liked it, I've taken a little inspiration from it myself for this site, but not too much. I was a little surprised how complex the proccess of exporting from Publii was, considering it was part of their brand that your work should be yours. I suppose in every other sense of the word it is. Hopefully they make exporting easier in a later release.

I was going to make a PHP scraper to dump the data into files and be done with it. But then I decided it might disturb the context of some of the posts, particularly where I mention my other website that is now this website. I had intended on exploring Publii more as well, but as I use a Raspberry Pi for computing, I was stuck on an older, unofficial release. I have an Intel device with the current version installed. But I'm not going to boot that up for one single task alone - although admittedly I will do that to play Sonic Mania on Steam.

I don't often use pictures for my blog - so I must remember to adjust the static site generator not to expect them ... and, done! It was just a simple case of adjusting a line in the PHP:

// Old
$imgUrl = $dom->querySelector('img')->getAttribute('src');

// New
$img = $dom->querySelector('img');
$imgUrl = $img !== null ? $img->getAttribute('src') : "";

And one in the feed.php template:

<!-- Old -->
<enclosure url="<?= $imgUrl ?>" type="image/jpeg" length="0" />
<media:thumbnail url="<?= $imgUrl ?>" width="1920" height="1080" />
<media:content url="<?= $imgUrl ?>" type="image/jpeg" />

<!-- New -->
<?php if (strlen($imgUrl) > 0): ?>
  <enclosure url="<?= $imgUrl ?>" type="image/jpeg" length="0" />
  <media:thumbnail url="<?= $imgUrl ?>" width="1920" height="1080" />
  <media:content url="<?= $imgUrl ?>" type="image/jpeg" />
<?php endif; ?>

Oh yeah, and I can include XML in my RSS feed on this site's version of my blog - which I couldn't in Publii due to the way it handled it's Atom feed. So expect more of that. Take that Publii!

item.title: PHP Static Site Generator
item.description: I'm learning PHP. I've wanted to learn it for a while but it's taken me a while to get around to actually starting. But I've started now, and even just as I start my journey, some of my misconceptions have been flipped upside down. I'm not saying you should learn it, but if you've been wanting to, and like I was, you are a little intimidated by it or don't know where to start, then hopefully this article might inspire you to just go for it.
item.content:encoded:
I'm learning PHP. I've wanted to learn it for a while but it's taken me a while to get around to actually starting. But I've started now, and even just as I start my journey, some of my misconceptions have been flipped upside down. I'm not saying you should learn it, but if you've been wanting to, and like I was, you are a little intimidated by it or don't know where to start, then hopefully this article might inspire you to just go for it.

It's something I've always been curious about, but the bar to entry appeared quite high previously. You need a server to run it, you need to know some system administration to run a server, you will probably need to learn Docker too. I've had a little exposure to PHP since setting up a NextCloud instance, and I recently set up a Coolify instance on a Raspberry Pi 4 so now I have somewhere cheap to play around with it and hopefully learn this language to a useful degree.

Now that I have begun learning it, and I should stress I have only just started - this is literally the first project I've done and I haven't even learned PHP Classes yet - I regret not having started sooner. You don't need a server to start learning PHP. This project generates a static HTML website (this website!) that at the time of writing is hosted on Github Pages. Sure, I had already done this in Python, but PHP has been designed for the web, and it is certainly evident in as much that as a total newb I have completed this entire project in a relatively short space of time, and in such a way that it is far more portable and customisable than it's Python counterpart.

Getting Started

If like me, you're running Linux, you've already taken the first step towards a LAMP stack without even trying. Windows and Mac users, I'm not in that world anymore, you'll need Google - my apologies. One thing I'm really enjoying about PHP is I don't have to install yet another package manager. I mean, there is Composer, but for this project at least, I haven't even had to give it a look yet. All the required dependencies were in the Debian Trixie apt repository.

sudo apt install php php-cli php-xml

That's it! php itself, php-cli to run the PHP from the command line as a script (this will be very useful in this project), and php-xml to parse and manipulate XML and HTML.

If you're using VS Code/Codium then the live-server plugin should run PHP fine (or at least it did last time I used it), and I imagine any sensible IDE or editor should be just as easy to get set up. I, however, am using Vim, and had to dig up some Vim script to get a working PHP server. Just put the following somewhere in your .vimrc if you are in the same same boat as me. Just use leader StartPHPServer to get a live PHP server going quickly in Vim.

" PHP LiveServer Start
function! StartPHPServer()
  let cmd = "php -S 127.0.0.1:8080 & firefox 127.0.01:8080 &"
  call system(cmd)
  echo "PHP server started in the background: 127.0.0.1:8080"
endfunction

function! StartPHPServerOnPort(port)
  let port_num = a:port + 0
  let cmd = "php -S 127.0.0.1:" . port_num . " & firefox 127.0.0.1:" . port_num . " &"
  call system(cmd)
  echo "PHP server started in the background on port " . port_num . ": 127.0.0.1" . port_num
endfunction

function! KillPHPServer()
  let cmd = "pkill -f 'php'"
  call system(cmd)
endfunction

augroup PHPServerKill
  autocmd!
  autocmd VimLeave * call KillPHPServer()
augroup END

command! StartPHPServer call StartPHPServer()
command! -nargs=1 StartPHPServerOnPort call StartPHPServerOnPort(<f-args>)
command! KillPHPServer call KillPHPServer()
" PHP LiveServer End

Setting Up A Simple Server

If you have used anything like Express in NodeJS or Flask in Python, this should all feel pretty familiar. We don't need anything particularly secure or rugged, the server will be primarily to have a live environment to work in while working on the website. The magic will happen when we call the same index.php script in the command line without a server running. Doing that will allow us to pipe the output (HTML) into files in a dist folder. I still use the Github Pages default docs folder for sake of simplicity, but I will use dist here for clarity.

Folder structure will loosely follow a MVC (Model View Controller) paradigm for organisation, but as I haven't learned PHP Classes yet I'm just throwing the whole thing together procedurally. Folder structure will have a public directory - this is where PHP looks by default for an index.php file. I'll also dump all my static content and root files in here too. An app folder will have anything functional such as controllers and helpers and a config folder for any settings, with a views folder for templates. Finally a src folder instead of models - since I'm generating a static site I will just be keeping my articles as stripped down HTML files, to be placed into a template as a HTML string.

project_root/
├── app/
├── config/
├── dist/
├── public/
|   ├── assets/
|   ├── images/
|   ├── CNAME
|   ├── robots.txt
|   └── index.php
├── src/
└── views/

In index.php we first need to define our paths. As we will be working on a live server, and building from command line, the script needs to be able to identify in which enviroment it is being run. We can do this with the php_sapi_name function. If the script is running from command line, url params will be swapped out for command line arguments, otherwise we can use the $_SERVER['PATH_INFO'] from the server to determine the route.

<?php

declare(strict_types=1);

$root = dirname(__DIR__) . DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR;

define('CONFIG_PATH', $root . 'config' . DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR);
define('APP_PATH', $root . 'app' . DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR);
define('SRC_PATH', $root . 'src' . DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR);
define('VIEWS_PATH', $root . 'views' . DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR);

require APP_PATH . 'App.php';

if (php_sapi_name() === 'cli') {
  $path = sizeof($argv) > 1 ? $argv[1] : null;
  $url = resolveUrl($path);
} else {
  $url = resolveUrl($_SERVER['PATH_INFO']);
}

if ($url['isFeed']) {
  feedController($url);
} else if ($url['isPost']) {
  postController($url);
} else if ($url['isBlog']) {
  blogController($url);
} else if ($url['path'] === '/') {
  homePageController();
} else {
  pageNotFoundController();
}

resolveUrl and the various route controllers are coming from app/App.php. resolveUrl is simply working out what route should be applied - a framework would parse url params for you usually, but I'm working from scratch here.

function getPath(string $uri): string
{
  $path = preg_replace('/\/+/', '/', $uri);
  $path = trim($path, '/');

  return $path;
}

function resolveUrl(string|null $uri): array
{
  $configs = include CONFIG_PATH . 'config.php';
  $url = array();

  if ($uri !== null) {
    $url['path'] = getPath($uri);
    $url['params'] = explode('/', $url['path']);
  } else {
    $url['path'] = '/';
    $url['params'] = array();
  }

  $url['isFeed'] = $url['params'] !== null
    && in_array('feed', $url['params']);

  $url['isBlog'] = $url['params'] !== null
    && in_array($url['params'][0], array_keys($configs['blogs']));

  $url['isPost'] = $url['isBlog']
    && $url['params'] !== null
    && sizeof($url['params']) > 1;

  return $url;
}

My website has a few different blogs: guides and tech. I am planning on adding my other actual blog into this site too. Each blog has it's own folder with an index.html file and the articles (previously HTML files but now folders containing index.html files in each). I explode the uri and check its parameters, to see if that is an existing blog - the list of blogs is stored in a config file. If it's a blog with no following params, it will go to it's index, if it has an existing param after the blog, then that param will be assumed to be a post, and a check is done to make sure that post exists. I can also check if it is looking for a feed path, or assign it the home path. If it is not the home path, and all other checks fail, the router will respond with the 404 page.

For now, we only need config/config.php to return an array of valid blogs. But I want to preserve the blog order, and use a consistent blog description in various places across my website so I have included those too.

<?php

$guidesDesc = fn (): string => "A description for Guides blog";
$techDesc = fn (): string => "A description for Tech blog";

return array(
  'blogs' => [
    'guides' => $guidesDesc(),
    'tech' => $techDesc()
  ],
  'blogOrder' => [
    'guides',
    'tech'
  ],
);

Serving a Blog Post

Now the server is routing requests, we need to handle the routes themselves using the controllers. The controllers are all in the App.php file in the app directory. Each one will collect and organise the required data before passing that data into the relevant template located in the views directory.

function postController(array $url): void
{
  require APP_PATH . 'helpers.php';
  $blog = $url['params'][0];
  $post = $url['params'][1];
  $src = SRC_PATH . $blog . DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR . $post . '.html';
  $content = getPost($blog, $post);
  $dom = Dom\HTMLDocument::createFromString($content);
  $postInfo = getPostInfo($dom);
  [
    'title' => $title,
    'description' => $description,
    'imgUrl' => $imgUrl,
    'date' => $date,
    'topics' => $topics,
    'sections' => $sections,
    'prismRequired' => $prismRequired
  ] = $postInfo;
  $jsonLd = getJsonLd($postInfo);

  require VIEWS_PATH . 'post.php';
}

The simplest task may be the displaying a single post page, so let's start with that one. In my postController function, I will first require helpers.php, where I am keeping code to help retreive, organise and manipulate data. A $blog and a $post variable are defined using the url parameters, and then the relevant post is fetched using a getPost function defined in helpers.php. getPost simply returns the HTML file contents as a string, which is then used to create an instance of the Dom\HTMLDocument class, which we can then send to the getPostInfo in helpers.php in order to cherry pick any information we might want to use later on. The function returns an associative array, so we simply unpack only the keys and values we require by destructuring the return value - we are handling a request for a blog post here, so unsurprisingly we are using all of the return values in this case. However, most of this data will be used to generate meta data, such as descriptions, the schema, and JSON Linked Data. Finally, once processed, the data will be passed into the views template post.php

function getPost(string $blog, string $post): string
{
  $src = SRC_PATH . $blog . DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR .$post . '.html';

  if (file_exists($src)) {
    $file = fopen($src, 'r') or die("Unable to open file");
    $content = fread($file, filesize($src));
    fclose($file);
    return $content;
  } else {
    return 'Error loading ' . $src;
  }
}

function getPostInfo(object $dom): array
{
  $title = $dom->querySelector('h1')->textContent;
  $description = $dom->querySelector('p#description')->textContent;
  $imgUrl = $dom->querySelector('img')->getAttribute('src');
  $date = $dom->querySelector('time')->getAttribute('datetime');
  $topics = $dom->querySelectorAll('li.topic');
  $sections = $dom->querySelectorAll('section');
  $prismRequired = preIsUsed($dom);

  return array(
    'title' => $title,
    'description' => $description,
    'imgUrl' => $imgUrl,
    'date' => $date,
    'topics' => $topics,
    'sections' => $sections,
    'prismRequired' => $prismRequired
  );
}

In only a handful of function calls form start to finish, we are ready to assemble our blog post's HTML using the relevant template php file in the views directory. In the interest of readability, I'm going to leave most stuff out. But here you will be able to see how simple it is to include the article inside of an article element just using the $content string. As mentioned, most of the additional data collected from the DOM is being used to populate meta data, but you can see here that I am using it to generate a page navigation if the article is split into sections. Sometimes I split articles up into parts, and sometimes I don't. Using PHP I don't have to consciously worry about how a page will be laid out, and all blog posts can use the same template regradless of their individual structure.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
  </head>

  <body>

<?php if ($sections->length > 0): ?>
  <nav aria-labelledby="page-nav">
    <header>
      <h2 id="page-nav">On This Page</h2>
    </header>
    <ol>
  <?php foreach ($sections as $section): ?>
    <li><a href="#<?= $section->getAttribute('id') ?>"><?= $section->getAttribute('title') ?></a></li>
  <?php endforeach; ?>
    </ol>
    </nav>
<?php endif; ?>

    <main>
      <article>
        <?= $content; ?>
      </article>
    </main>

  </body>
</html>

Serving a Blog

Now we are serving our blog posts, we can take a look at serving the blog reel itself. Exactly how you do this will depend a bit on preference and taste, but I like to have a separate blog reel for each of my blogs. I can use a single template to generate any of my blogs using PHP. The blogs in config.php will be of great help here, as it can provide the description for each blog so that I can use it in page, as well as including the descriptions on the home page, in page meta, as well as in the RSS feeds. Let's start by taking a look at the blogController function in App.php.

function blogController(array $url): void
{
  $configs = include CONFIG_PATH . 'config.php';
  require APP_PATH . 'helpers.php';
  $blog = $url['params'][0];
  $blogDesc = $configs['blogs'][$blog];
  $posts = getBlogPosts($blog);
  uasort($posts, "newestPost");

  require VIEWS_PATH . 'blog.php';
}

This one looks a little simpler than the postController function, if only because it doesn't have to destructure anything. Blogs will still need to be destructured, but to reduce the work load I will take care of that within the template while iterating over the relevant blog posts. For now, the function simply determines which blog it is looking for using the url parameter, collects the required blog description from the config file, collects the relevant blogs by calling a getBlogPosts function, and then uses PHP's built in uasort function to sort the posts using the callback newestPost function. getBlogPosts and newestPost are both defined in helpers.php

function getBlogPosts(string $blog): array
{
  $dir = SRC_PATH . $blog . DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR; 
  $files = scandir($dir);
  $posts = array();

  foreach ($files as $file) {
    $path = $dir . $file;

    if (is_file($path) && substr($file, -5) === '.html') {
      $dom = Dom\HTMLDocument::createFromFile($path);
      $postName = str_replace('.html', '', $file);
      $posts[$postName] = [
        'dom' => $dom,
        'blog' => $blog
      ];
    }
  }

  return $posts;
}
  
function newestPost(array $a, array $b): int
{
  $ad = $a['dom']->querySelector('time')->getAttribute('datetime');
  $bd = $b['dom']->querySelector('time')->getAttribute('datetime');

  if ($ad === $bd) {
    return 0;
  }

  return ($ad > $bd) ? -1 : 1;
}

The getBlogPosts function is passed a blog string which it uses to set the correct directory, then checks each file is valid and adds it to an associated array using the extension-stripped filename as it's key and a dom object and the blog string as key value pairs, and finally returns the array. By checking that the file ends in ".html" we can prevent picking up invalid filetypes such as the swap files that editors like vim might generate when a file has a buffer active. The blog key value pair is not important in this particular workflow, but will prove helpful when working with more than one blog at a time, such as on the home page or in the main RSS feed.

The newestPost callback used in the uasort simply picks the date out of the articles time element and compares it to it's neighbour in the array.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
  </head>
  <body>
    <header>
    </header>

    <main>
      <header>
        <h1><?= ucfirst($blog) ?></h1>
        <p><?= $blogDesc ?></p>
      </header>
    
      <nav id="articles">
<?php foreach($posts as $postName => $post):

  $postInfo = getPostInfo($post['dom']);
  [
  'title' => $title,
  'description' => $description,
  'date' => $date,
  'topics' => $topics
  ] = $postInfo;

  $url = '/' . $blog . '/' . $postName;
?>

        <article>
          <header>
            <h3><a href="<?= $url ?>"><?= $title ?></a></h3>
            <time datetime="<?= $date ?>"><?= formatDate($date); ?></time>
            <ul class="topic-container">
  <?php foreach($topics as $topic): ?>
              <li class="topic"><?= $topic->textContent ?></li>
  <?php endforeach ?>
            </ul>
          </header>
          <p class="description"><?= $description ?></p>
          <a href="<?= $url ?>">Read More</a>
        </article>
<?php endforeach ?>
      </nav>
    </main>

    <script src="/assets/scripts/filter.js"></script>
  </body>
</html>

Once again, I've stripped out a lot of the stuff that doesn't matter. What happens here, is first we simply populate a title and description for the particular blog - I use the PHP built in function ucfirst to uppercase the first letter of the blog title. Then we iterate over each post in the associative array, which has already been sorted by newest first, and use the getPostInfo function we used for the blog post earlier, to destructure what we need for each post - we don't need a lot here, only the title, description, date and topics. We also use the $blog and postName strings to generate the url - $blog was defined within our controller function, and $postName is the key for the particular post. Once that is done, we have everything we need to create a link for each post with a date and description, as well is a list of topics, which I use with JavaScript to automatically generate a filter search for each blog based on the topics pinned to each article.

Serving an RSS Feed

Next, we will look at how to serve an RSS feed. There are, of course, other pages that I will be serving and generating within my site, but there isn't really anything new to gain from looking at those. However, when serving XML, I encountered a few caveats and gotchas, so I thought I would share the solution I ended up going with. When researching solutions, I came across a few different ones. There may be bettter solutions than mine, and I haven't had mine in production long enough to find bugs yet, but for me this method felt fast and familiar, and didn't deviate too much from what I had already been doing elsewhere in the code. Let's begin by taking a look at what the feedController function is doing.

function feedController(array $url): void
{
  $configs = include CONFIG_PATH . 'config.php';
  require APP_PATH . 'helpers.php';
  $posts = array();

  if ($url['isBlog']) {
    $blog = $url['params'][0];
    $posts = [...getBlogPosts($blog)];
  } else {
    foreach ($configs['blogs'] as $blog => $blogDesc) {
      $posts += [...getBlogPosts($blog)];
    }
  }

  uasort($posts, "newestPost");

  require VIEWS_PATH . 'feed.php';
}

Again, not drastically different from what we've seen before - unsurprising, as we are once again dealing with blog posts in some fashion. This simply checks if a blog has been specified, if one has it will add all the posts from that blog to an associative array and then sort the array using he newestPost callback function. If a blog has not been specified, and we have been routed to the feed controller, then it stands to reason that we need to serve the main feed that includes posts from all of the blogs. There isn't anything new to look at in here, so next we can move straight into the feed template.

<?php
header('Content-Type: application/xml; charset=utf-8');
echo '<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>' . PHP_EOL;
?>
<rss xmlns:atom="http://www.w3.org/2005/Atom" xmlns:media="http://search.yahoo.com/mrss/" xmlns:content="http://purl.org/rss/1.0/modules/content/" version="2.0">
  <channel>
  <atom:link href="https://aaronwatts.dev/<?= $url['isBlog'] ? $blog . '/' : '' ?>feed.xml" rel="self" type="applications/rss+xml" />
    <title>AaronWattsDev <?= $url['isBlog'] ? ucfirst($blog) : 'Latest'  ?></title>
    <link>https://aaronwatts.dev<?= $url['isBlog'] ? '/' . $blog : '' ?>/</link>
    <description><?= $blogDesc ?></description>
    <category>Technology</category>
<?php
$x = 0;
foreach($posts as $postName => $post):
  $x++;
  if ($x > 10) {
    break;
  }

  $postInfo = getPostInfo($post['dom']);
  [
    'title' => $title,
    'description' => $description,
    'imgUrl' => $imgUrl,
    'date' => $date,
    'topics' => $topics,
    'sections' => $sections,
    'prismRequired' => $prismRequired
  ] = $postInfo;

  $src = SRC_PATH . $post['blog'] . DIRECTORY_SEPARATOR .$postName . '.html';
  
  if (file_exists($src)) {
    $file = fopen($src, 'r') or die("Unable to open file!");
    $content = fread($file, filesize($src));
    fclose($file);
    $content = preg_replace('/<header>(.|\n)*?<\/header>/', '', $content);
    $content = str_replace(['<', '>'], ['<', '>'], $content);
  }
  
  $baseUrl = 'https://aaronwatts.dev';
  $url = $baseUrl . '/' . $post['blog'] . '/' . $postName;
?>
    <item>
      <title><?= $title ?></title>
      <link><?= $url ?></link>
      <pubDate><?= date('r', strtotime($date)); ?></pubDate>
      <description><?= $description ?></description>
      <guid><?= $url ?></guid>
      <content:encoded><?= trim($content) ?></content:encoded>
      <enclosure url="<?= $imgUrl ?>" type="image/jpeg" length="0" />
      <media:thumbnail url="<?= $imgUrl ?>" width="1920" height="1080" />
      <media:content url="<?= $imgUrl ?>" type="image/jpeg" />
    </item>
<?php endforeach; ?>
  </channel>
</rss>

Visually, there's a bit more going on here than in the previous templates. The first thing to note is the built-in PHP header function at the beginning. PHP expects to serve HTML by default. To serve an XML file, this needs to be included in the header of the HTTP response so that the browser knows what filetype it is working with. Next I had to echo the first line on the XML file. I'm not entirely sure why I could only get it to work this way, hopefully it will start to make sense the more PHP I learn. With those two gotcha's out of the way we can handle the rest of the file as though it were any other PHP template.

I'm using the same feed.php file for the RSS feed for each blog, as well as the aggregated all blog. So I need to include some ternary logic to handle all cases for the feeds information. Then I can iterate over the items in the blog array that I put together in the feedController function. I'm limiting my feeds to 10 articles each, and that is handled within the loop using a break statement, so if there were less than 10 posts then the loop would just end of it's own accord without breaking anything in the script.

Building the Site

I have a few more pages on my website, but with what we have looked at, we have all the concepts required to make a home page, sitemap XML file, and whatever else we need. So with the bulk of the work out of the way, we can make a build script.

For the build script, I chose to use BASH. I like BASH, but I don't get to use it a whole lot, so I'm not particularly good at it. But we only need to run some sequential tasks for the build process.

#!/bin/bash

PROJECT_ROOT=$( cd -- "$( dirname -- "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}" )" &> /dev/null && pwd )
PHP_PUBLIC="${PROJECT_ROOT}/public"
PHP_RUN="${PHP_PUBLIC}/index.php"
BLOGS_DIR="${PROJECT_ROOT}/src"
BUILD_DIR="${PROJECT_ROOT}/dist"

# Write home page to index.html
php "$PHP_RUN" > "${BUILD_DIR}/index.html"

# Write collated feed
php "$PHP_RUN" "feed" > "${BUILD_DIR}/feed.xml"

# Write blog pages, posts and blog feeds
for blogDir in "${BLOGS_DIR}"/*;
do
  blog="$(basename "${blogDir}")"
  php "$PHP_RUN" "$blog" > "${BUILD_DIR}/${blog}/index.html"
  php "$PHP_RUN" "${blog}/feed" > "${BUILD_DIR}/${blog}/feed.xml"

  for postFile in "${blogDir}"/*;
  do
    post="$(basename "${postFile}" .html)"
    mkdir "${BUILD_DIR}/${blog}/${post}"
    php "$PHP_RUN" "${blog}/${post}" > "${BUILD_DIR}/${blog}/${post}/index.html"
  done;
done;

# Copy root files and folders
for name in "${PHP_PUBLIC}"/*;
do
  if [ "$name" != "${PHP_PUBLIC}/index.php" ]; then
    if [ -d "$name" ]; then
      cp -R "$name" "$BUILD_DIR";
    elif [ -f "$name" ]; then
      cp "$name" "$BUILD_DIR";
    fi
  fi;
done;

The script isn't very complicated, although I still managed to eat my RAM and freeze my laptop while writing it. After setting our directories we simply run the php script, using arguments in place of a URI. We use the BASH > operator to write the PHP script's return value to a file, or replace the existing contents with the return value if the file already exists. We do this for each blog page, blog feed, and each post within their respective blogs. Finally, we just copy anything in our public directory directly into the root of the dist directory.

And with that, the static HTML files are ready to be served wherever you might choose to do so. There is certainly more that can be done here, but we have a working static site generator with PHP on our local machine and no need for a server. I hope that after reading this, anyone who might have been considering learning PHP but felt intimidated or overwhelmed by it, will feel a bit better about just diving into it.

item.title: NextCloud
item.description: NextCloud is a cloud storage solution that is intended as privacy focused with an option for self hosting. I've been using it for a while now, and I am very happy with it.
item.content:encoded:
NextCloud is a cloud storage solution that is intended as privacy focused with an option for self hosting. I've been using it for a while now, and I am very happy with it.

NextCloud is an alternative to things like Google Drive and One Drive that doesn't hand your data and the control over to a conglomerate. Self hosting is not the simplest thing to do, but there are also providers available that do all the hard stuff for you so you can just get on with having a cloud.

Originally, I was subscribed to Murena's Workspace cloud plan. I didn't have a Murena phone, but the NextCloud offer looked quite good so I tried it. I was pleased, the WorkSpace is pretty good, and includes an OnlyOffice suite for online editing. A measly €1.99 per month gets you 20GB of storage, or you can get 64GB for just €3.99. However, they had some issues a while back when upgrading their infrastructure, and their cloud went down. It's back up now, and due to the way NextCloud syncs with devices, I had local backups on several devices so I didn't lose any files.

But the downtime was a bit longer than anticipated, and during that time I thought I might try set up my own cloud on a VPS. And I did, successfully. I pay a lot more for my NextCloud on a VPS setup, but I get total control of what apps I have on my server. That said, I also have total responsibility when things stop working, which has happened.

Installation is not simple, there are All-In-One installations which are supposed to make things easier, available as either a Snap package or a Docker image, but for me (a novice) the documentation didn't seem to match up and I couldn't get everything working.

If you have some experience in the Linux terminal, then I highly suggest following along to the Learn Linux guide, which is also available as a YouTube walthrough (linked in article). Jay does a great job of explaining what he is doing and why, and if you've ever poked around in PHP applications it should feel quite familiar. I genuinely felt like I had learned quite a bit after working through the guide, as opposed to mindlessly following steps to acheive a goal.

I wasn't able to apply a recent update, and had to reinstall the software, and some steps had changed, but I was able to figure them out on my own as I kind of understood what I was supposed to be doing. Nonetheless, I wouldn't describe the process as easy. And keeping your cloud maintained will also require some work. So if you want to try it, but don't have the time or patience to go through the set up and maintainence, then take a look for a provider.

As an alternative to other cloud providers, NextCloud is actually really good. There is a huge community making stuff for it. At it's most basic it will back up files to the cloud and sync with any number of devices you want it to, giving you local backups if anything was to go wrong. There's a plethora of compatible software for it, and getting your phone sync'd to it is pretty easy too. I'm currently using it as my Documents folder on two computers, so everything I'm working on is accessible anywhere. I also have my git repositories on it, and have had no issues with those. I'm also using it as the directories for software like Publii CMS and Calibre Library, so my blogs and books are available at whatever computer I'm working at.

item.title: Raspberry Pi
item.description: Since it's early days, the Raspberry Pi ecosystem has become huge, monolithic even. item.content:encoded:
Since it's early days, the Raspberry Pi ecosystem has become huge, monolithic even. I remember picking up my first one from a UK high street store called Maplin many years ago through curiousity. It was a Raspberry Pi 2 Model B, and it didn't work. I went through a 12 month process of arguing for a replacement on warranty, and the parcel being delivered to the wrong address. I had forgotten all about it when a neighbour returned from an extended trip abroad, and brought the box to my door.

You're probably expecting the next line to be something along the lines of "I have been tinkering ever since". Well, no, actually. At that time in my life I had a penchant for the outdoors, and a not particularly well paid job working at a charity. I didn't have a dedicated computer at the time, only a Playstation 3 (as well as my retro consoles that were entirely off line at that point) that I had bought second hand. Beyond being a very underpowered Linux computer, I wasn't totally sure what this thing called a Raspberry Pi was meant to be.

Eventually my cirumstances changed, I moved career, got a computer, and became aquainted with the internet. I still had my collection of retro gaming consoles, and had a bit of side hustle on the go buying games and consoles at deals, restoring them if they needed it, and selling them on. I was feeding a hobby and making some money on the side, and perhaps contributing to the ridiculous prices that retro gaming would eventually hold - sorry about that.

Naturally, the omniscient Youtube algorithm knew what I wanted to watch before I even did (some of the time), and I kept seeing videos of emulation. A video caught my eye, likely a guide on how to install RetroPie onto this device I had sitting in my drawer. Okay, so that's what that thing can do. Nice! I had most of the real world consoles, with most of the games that I wanted for them. So while I didn't run out the door to buy a USB controller, I did get curious to what else this machine could do. And that's when I began tinkering, and have been ever since.

I understood: it might not have been powerful enough to replace a desktop computer, but it was very good at doing one thing, and doing it really well. To try and list all the things you could do with a Raspberry Pi would be, frankly, a little ridiculous. As I have already mentioned, the ecosystem is huge. There's heaps of talented people in the community, and resources have become immense. Some of the projects I have kept around (some of which there are guides for on this website) include:

  • Retro gaming console
  • Handheld retro gaming console
  • KDE Bigscreen smart TV
  • Web radio with touch screen using Volumio

These are just a few I have kept around. I have also experimented with running servers and sinkholes on my Raspberry Pi 2, had Kodi and Magic Mirror running on my Pi 3, and explored various operating systems across the devices too. I haven't even mentioned the Model A or Zero devices, or the Pico Micro Controllers, or robotics, or drones, or AI, or home automation .. you get the message.

Later, the Raspberry Pi 5 family would make desktop computing entirely comfortable. I use a Raaspberry Pi 500+ as my main computer at my desk, and a Compute Module 5, in the new Argon One Up laptop sysem (which I am working at now, while I type this!). Desktop computing was an okay experience on the Raspberry Pi 4, although with the demands of modern software (particularly browsers), you needed to maintain an austere process and sacrifice a little multi-tasking.

We’re on a mission to put high-performance, low-cost, general-purpose computing platforms in the hands of enthusiasts and engineers all over the world.

Raspberry Pi is not the only Single Board Computer out there. But it is arguably the most prolific and may have had the biggest impact on hobbyist computing. Low cost, low energy, and the ability to keep reusing old hardware means that it is all potentially very sustainable. SBC's have placed a little of the power into the hands of consumers that want to tinker and play. SBC's are to software what Lego is to architecture. Except if you build a house from Lego you can't live in it, whereas if you build software or a useful device with an SBC, you can absolutely use it.

Raspberry Pi is an engine for creativity, learning and innovation. With over sixty million of our computers sold in the last decade, there has never been a more exciting time to build on Raspberry Pi.

As for tech I consider to be thoughtful, I think the Raspberry Pi is a serious contender for the most thoughtful tech. By proffession I am a youth worker, and occassionally a kid I work with will mention learning to code on a Raspberry Pi, and that just makes me smile!

item.title: Better Meta
item.description: I have another website, that I manage with CMS (Content Management Software). I haven't bothered setting up anything for Google or Bing indexing for that site yet, I was waiting to see if I would keep using the site first. But content I was putting on that site was getting indexed anyway, and it also looked good in the search results. So I decided to investigate why this was the case.
item.content:encoded:
I have another website, that I manage with CMS (Content Management Software). I haven't bothered setting up anything for Google or Bing indexing for that site yet, I was waiting to see if I would keep using the site first. But content I was putting on that site was getting indexed anyway, and it also looked good in the search results. So I decided to investigate why this was the case.

SEO. Isn't it always the answer? I put my hands up, I'm not an expert on it, it's quite a broad subject. I prefer playing in a terminal. But if a website can get itself indexed on it's own, to a high standard and without any human hands getting involved, then it's worth knowing about.

NOTE: Keep in mind, this relies on web crawler bots coming to your site. So while it automates page indexing, if you want things done fast you may still want to use other methods.

Robots

Let's start with the simplest thing first. The robots.txt file. I've only read about this file being used to limit web crawler activity on a website. It seems obvious now I've seen it, but if it can tell robots to go away, then it can also tell them to come in.

User-agent: *
Disallow:
Sitemap: https://aaronwatts.dev/sitemap.xml

There we go: all crawlers welcome, here's my site directory. I had been using an XSL template for my sitemap previously, which has since broken on Chromium. Chromium is in the process of removing XSL support from the blink web engine, I'm not sure if that's likely to effect certain web crawlers too, but just to be safe I have removed the XSL instruction from the XML sitemap file.

OpenGraph

The OpenGraph protocol is a standard that allows relevant information to be picked out by social media applications to generate thumbnails. Not dissimilar from the standard meta description tag, but richer.

Making use of the tool is just a case of adding the necessary meta elements to your document head.

<html>
  <head>
    <meta property="og:title" content="Better Meta"/>
    <meta property="og:site_name" content="aaronwatts@dev"/>
    <meta property="og:description" content="intro text here"/>
    <meta property="og:url" content="https://aaronwatts.dev/guides/better-meta"/>
    <meta property="og:image" content="https://aaronwatts.dev/images/guides/better-meta.avif"/>
    <meta property="og:type" content="article"/>
    <meta property="og:article:published_time" content="2026-03-05"/>
  </head>
  ...
</html>

The content required for the tags already all exists somewhere within the document itself, so this can all be done programmatically, which I will look at shortly. Automating the process also redduces the risk of breaking something with a typo.

Twitter has an OpenGraph property for it's cards, which I am not currently implementing here, but will do soon. I have used this page as an example, which would count as an article, but the schema is vast, and it's worth consulting the documentation for what kind of clues you can provide, about what type of content your material is, to other sites that might display links to your site.

Schema

Similar to OpenGraph, there are also rich content identifiers specifically for search engines. Google, along with other search engines, use the schema.org vocabulary.

The easiest way to work with schema is using json-ld (JSON Linked Data). Some schema classifications have required attributes, and Google's developer documentation has helpful guidance and what ought to be included, and what is complimentary.

<html>
  <head>
    <script type="application/ld+json">{
      "@context": "http://schema.org",
      "@type": "Article",
      "mainEntityOfPage": {
        "@type": "WebPage",
        "@id": "https://aaronwatts.dev/guides/better-meta"
      },
      "headline": "Better Meta",
      "datePublished": "2025-03-05",
      "description": "intro text here",
      "image": [
        "https://aaronwatts.dev/images/guides/better-meta.avif"
      ],
      "author": {
        "@type": "Person",
        "name": "aaronwatts@dev"
      }
    }</script>
  </head>
  ...
</html>

To implement a schema using json-ld, you just need a script tag in the head of the document, with a type attribute of application/ld+json. As with the data required to populate the OpenGraph content, all the required data is contained somewhere within the document, so it can be done programmatically.

Automating the Process

If you are using a CMS, this stuff is likely being handled for you. But if not, it can be automated. How you acheive this will depend on the tech stack you use for a given website, and your preferred or available technologies. A PHP-like templating engine will be the simplest way to automate. For my use case, I have already made a CMS module in Python, and so have implemented the automation into that. Without looking too deeply into my CMS module, I'll outline how I have automated updating the meta for my articles using Python.

<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8"/>
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0"/>
  <meta name="description"/>
  ...
  <meta property="og:title"/>
  <meta property="og:site_name" content="aaronwatts@dev"/>
  <meta property="og:description"/>
  <meta property="og:url"/>
  <meta property="og:image"/>
  <meta property="og:type" content="article"/>
  <meta property="og:article:published_time"/>

  <script type="application/ld+json"></script>
</head>

Before I even run any Python code, my HTML documents for my articles will already contain the necessary OpenGraph meta tags and an empty script tag with a type of application/ld+json. Anything that is page specific will not have any data applied yet for the content attributes. I am also programmatically populating the content attribute for the standard meta description too for consistency. When I run my Python CMS module, it will first run a series of tests on each document and make sure the tags it is expecting to work with are all present in the document. If anything is missing, or other tests fail, it will exit the program and log what tests have failed.

def extract_data(doc):
  doc['title'] = doc['soup'].select_one(SELECTORS['title']).text
  doc['intro'] = doc['soup'].select_one(SELECTORS['intro']).text
  doc['description'] = " ".join(doc['intro'].split())
  doc['html_date'] = doc['soup'].select_one(SELECTORS['time'])
  doc['date_attr'] = doc['html_date']['datetime']
  doc['URL'] = path_to_url(f"{doc['directory']}/{doc['filename']}")
  doc['IMG'] = BASE_URL + selector(doc['soup'], "article img", "src")
  return doc

My CMS already iterates through documents to extract the required data to be able to create the RSS feeds, and add new articles to the index pages. So I already have all my data readily available. There are custom functions here to build a url from a specified file path, and a selector function to get an attributes content (I am not using that function to get the datetime attribute as I also use the html_date to format dates to RFC 822 for the RSS feed). My CSS selectors are all pulled out of a config file, so if I decide to change my document structure, I just need to alter the config file and not the code itself. The doc being passed into the function is a dictionary for each article document, with keys and values for filename, directory, and soup.

NOTE: I've only included the relevant extractions in the function above. More data gets extracted from each document, but they are not relevant to building the meta for the page and are instead used elsewhere, such as the RSS feeds.

def add_meta_content(article):
  head = selector(article['soup'], "head")

  description = selector(head, "meta[name='description']")
  description['content'] = article['description']

  og_title = selector(head, "meta[property='og:title']")
  og_title['content'] = article['title']
  og_desc = selector(head, "meta[property='og:description']")
  og_desc['content'] = article['description']
  og_url = selector(head, "meta[property='og:url']")
  og_url['content'] = article['URL']
  og_image = selector(head, "meta[property='og:image']")
  og_image['content'] = article['IMG']
  og_time = selector(head, "meta[property='og:article:published_time']")
  og_time['content'] = article['date_attr']

  json_ld = selector(head, "script[type='application/ld+json']")
  json_ld_data = {
    "@context": "http://schema.org",
    "@type": "Article",
    "mainEntityOfPage":{
      "@type": "WebPage",
      "@id": article['URL']
    },
    "headline": article['title'],
    "datePublished": article['date_attr'],
    "description": article['description'],
    "image": [
      article['IMG']
        ],
    "author":{
          "@type": "Person",
          "name": "aaronwatts@dev"
    }
  }

  json_ld_str = json.dumps(json_ld_data, indent=2)
  json_ld.string = json_ld_str

The extended article data is then passed into a function that populates the required meta tags with the applicable data. The Python json module is used to convert a Python dictionary into a JSON string.

article_path = f"{ROOT}/{article['directory']}/{article['filename']}"
write_to_html(article['soup'], article_path)

def write_to_html(soup, path):
  with open(path, "w") as outf:
    outf.write(str(soup))

Each document's soup retains all adjustments made, so the final step is simply to write the modified soup back into the file it has been taken from.
